units.translation: where the scholiast says: ἀφ' ἑαυτῶν ἔχοντα τὴν λαβὴν ξίφη [swords having their hilts from themselves], from which the Hesychian glosses αὐτόλαβον, ἑαυτοῦ λαβὴν ἔχον [self-hilted, having its own hilt], Abreschius restored the lemma as αὐτόκωπον [self-hilted], omitted through the fault of Hesychius himself, as the order of the letters shows.
swords having their hilts from themselves
I learn from my eyes, being my own witness of the return.

Thus I corrected what is read in M from the gloss ἰδίᾳ γνώμᾳ [by one's own judgment]. See the Preface to the fifth Leipzig edition p. XIX. In another sense, 'the mind itself', the philosophers said αὐτόνους (or αὐτονοῦς) [self-minded]: see Thes. vol. 1, 2 p. 2544, where add Euseb. Pr. Ev. 7 p. 327 a.
With self-willed judgment you honor mortals too much, Prometheus.
the land—which they allotted to me root and branch, to the full.
making the journey on one's own feet
making the journey on one's own feet

Thus I corrected what is in M: αὐτὸν ὡς ἀκούομεν [him as we hear], about which I spoke in Philologus vol. 13 p. 476 477. The same is said in other words below at 734: μονάδα δὲ Ξέρξην ἔρημόν φασιν οὐ πολλῶν μέτα | ἄσμενον μολεϊν γέρυραν γαῖν δυοῖν ζευκτηρίαν [they say Xerxes, alone and deserted, not with many, came gladly to the bridge, the yoke of the two continents]. Pauwius had noticed the fault of the vulgate reading, who conjectured αὐτὸν εἰσακούομεν [we hear him], not realizing that εἰσακούομεν [we hear] is less suitable to this passage than the simple verb ἀκούομεν [we hear].
We hear that the king escaped with little, on his own feet.
they say Xerxes, alone and deserted, not with many, came gladly to the bridge, the yoke of the two continents

"It should be read — ὅσον ἑαυτὸν ἔρεξε καὶ κατέθυσε. ἢ αὐτορέγμονος παρὰ τὸ ὀρέγειν τὴν χεῖρα [as much as he wrought and sacrificed himself. Or of self-wrought from stretching out the hand]. The grammarian proposes two etymologies of the word, one by which it is derived from αὐτός [self] and ῥέζειν [to do], the other by which from ὀρέγειν [to stretch]." L. DINDORF in the Thesaurus vol. 3 p. 11.
self-wrought: working oneself. Of a self-wrought fate: as much as he wrought and straightway self-wrought, from stretching out the hand, Aeschylus in the Cretan Women (fr. 117).
as much as he wrought and sacrificed himself. Or of self-wrought from stretching out the hand

This pronoun has a double meaning: first, 'self', by which a person or thing is distinguished from another person or thing, which, although it is everywhere evident by itself, is nevertheless not rarely expressed more explicitly by the addition of οὐκ ἄλλος [no other]; second (excluding the nominative case, which is used only in the former meaning), 'he, she, it', by which the person or thing spoken of in the preceding words is designated.
